chunks: Servo motor applications. The question: What are its applications?
Servos are used wherever something must sit at a chosen position, or follow a chosen motion, and stay accurate even when the load pushes back.
Examples run from a model-airplane flap to a factory robot arm. If you only need to spin something at a steady speed, use a plain motor.
If you only need a short on-off push, use a solenoid.
Think of the steering in a car. You turn the wheel to an angle and the wheels must hold that angle, even when bumps shove them.
That is a servo job: a position, held against disturbances. The ceiling fan above you only needs to spin, and a door latch only needs one quick push.
Neither needs to know a position, so a servo would be wasted on them.
A rough decision chart. Servos win when position or trajectory matters and the load is not guaranteed to be benign, because only a closed loop knows when it has failed to arrive.
Servo: a motor with a sensor and controller that goes to a commanded position and holds it. Trajectory: a path of positions over time, which the servo is asked to follow.
Disturbance rejection: pushing back when something tries to move the output. Torque: the twisting effort at the joint, in newton-meters (N·m).
Stall torque: the most torque the servo gives at zero speed. It is not the torque you can use continuously. Solenoid: a coil that gives a short on-off push.
A robot arm holds a 0. 5 kg payload 0. 30 m from the joint. With the arm horizontal, the joint must supply 0. 5 times 9. 81 times 0. 30 equals 1. 47 N·m.
The arm's own weight raises that to about 1. 9 N·m. Pick a servo with at least double that for acceleration and margin, roughly 3. 8 N·m of stall torque.
That is the whole idea: say what the job needs, then size from torque.

"Servos go wherever something has to be at a position or follow a trajectory and hold it against load: RC steering and control surfaces, robot arm joints, camera pan-tilts and gimbals, CNC and 3D printer axes, pick-and-place machines, throttle and valve actuators.
I'd use a servo when I need angle or trajectory with disturbance rejection. A plain motor is for constant speed and a solenoid for on-off strokes.
Sizing starts with joint torque, force times lever arm, with about 2x margin."
